What a Structural Scope Should Cover Before You Build

A BOQ can help a homeowner plan quantities and cost, but it is not a structural design. Before excavation or procurement, the project needs a qualified engineer's site-specific drawings and scope.

Start with the information the engineer needs

Bring the plot dimensions, architectural drawings, proposed number of floors, intended use of rooms, site photographs, and any soil or boundary information you have. This prevents an early estimate from being mistaken for a final design. If the plot has unusual soil, a slope, a basement, or an adjacent deep excavation, ask whether additional investigation is required.

What to expect in a useful scope

  • Foundation assumptions and the information used to select them.
  • Member drawings and a clear schedule for slabs, beams, columns, footings, and reinforcement.
  • Concrete and steel specifications, cover requirements, and details for openings and staircases.
  • Coordination notes for plumbing sleeves, electrical openings, water tanks, and later modifications.
  • A revision process: who approves changes and how the drawings are reissued.

Use the BOQ as a comparison tool

Once drawings are issued, use a BOQ to compare like-for-like quotations. Keep the drawing revision, material grade, unit, quantity, waste allowance, transport, and labour scope beside each line item. A cheaper quote that excludes shuttering, testing, or cartage is not necessarily cheaper after work starts.

Questions worth asking before work begins

Ask which drawings are approved for construction, who will answer site queries, how substitutions are documented, and whether the contractor will provide bar-bending schedules and concrete test records. Put answers in writing. These records make it easier to trace a change before it becomes a cost dispute.

Important: This is a planning checklist, not engineering advice. Engage a licensed, qualified professional for the structural design and local approvals for your project.
